structure.title: A voice arguing
structure.text: Part One presents the Underground Man's claims about reason, freedom, desire, and his own contradictory character.

structure.title: Encounters remembered
structure.text: Part Two recounts earlier social episodes. Concrete interactions put the preceding claims under a different kind of pressure.

people.name: The Underground Man
people.text: A forty-year-old former civil servant living alone in a shabby St Petersburg room, spiteful, ashamed and perversely proud of it.

people.name: His imagined audience
people.text: The 'gentlemen' he keeps addressing, sensible believers in reason and progress, whose objections he imagines and mocks in advance.

people.name: Liza
people.text: A young prostitute he meets late one night, to whom he lectures about her future and then cannot let go of.

context.title: An unreliable self-explanation
context.text: He can expose his motives and still misrepresent their implications. Self-criticism can become another way to retain control of the encounter.

passages.quote: I am a sick man.... I am a spiteful man.

context.title: Rational self-interest
context.text: Part One answers the Russian radicals of the 1860s, above all Chernyshevsky's novel What Is to Be Done? (1863), which held that people who understood their true interest would act on it. The crystal palace the narrator mocks is that novel's image of a rational future.
context.takeaway: Examine the examples, not only the slogans.

notice.why: The voice keeps trying to decide how its listener may respond.

notice.text: Follow money and gestures of kindness.
notice.why: Ordinary exchanges expose needs his theories cannot contain.

opening: The Underground Man would rather ruin an evening than let someone think he wanted their friendship. He nurses insults, rehearses revenge, and longs for affection he can barely bring himself to accept. He knows how petty he is being and can make a devastating argument against himself without changing his behaviour. Dostoevsky lets him explain, until the explanation itself becomes part of the trouble: a man clever enough to see through his own excuses keeps finding reasons to go on living by them.
